status: draft — physics not yet independently reviewed (master-project-prompt.md §31–§32)
prerequisites: All of Lessons 1–11 — this lesson assumes every framework in the unit
Newton's second law on a chosen axis, two-axis problems, connected systems (Lessons 4, 5, 8)
Newton's third law: interaction pairs vs balanced forces (Lesson 6)
Gravitation, springs, apparent weight, force–extension graphs (Lesson 9)
majorObjective: Consolidate the unit by deciding — with no cue — which framework a problem needs, then executing it. Four recurring problem types: a multi-force object (often on an incline, often with an angled applied force); a multi-object interaction (attribute every force, tell third-law pairs from balanced forces); a circular-motion scenario (name the real radial forces, apply $\sum F_r = mv^2/r$, check a limiting case); and a force–extension dataset (find $k$ from a slope, predict an untested value). This is the on-ramp to the unit test bank, where items are interleaved and you choose the tool.
subObjectives: Given an uncued problem, identify which framework applies from its structure — an object accelerating along a surface, an interaction between objects, motion on a curved path, or a proportional force–deformation relationship.
For a multi-force object: draw the free-body diagram, choose axes that match the acceleration, resolve off-axis forces, and solve $\sum F = ma$ on each axis.
For a multi-object interaction: attribute every force to its source, identify third-law pairs (two objects, same interaction) versus balanced forces (one object), and analyse system then part.
For circular motion: identify the real force(s) whose net points to the centre, apply $\sum F_r = mv^2/r$, and reason about a limiting case (max speed, string breaks, top vs bottom).
For a force–extension dataset: read $k$ as the slope, predict a force or displacement for an untested value, and state the linear-range assumption.
Run a reasonableness check on every result: units, limiting cases, sign/direction, rough size.

hook.prompt: A problem gives you a mass, a speed, a radius, and a coefficient of friction, and asks 'will the car make the turn?'. Before any numbers, the single most useful first move is:
choices: plug every given number into $F = ma$
recognise this as a circular-motion problem: the net inward force must equal $mv^2/r$, and friction (capped at $\mu_s mg$) is what supplies it
assume the car is in equilibrium because its speed is constant
convert everything to base SI units and wait for a formula

priorKnowledge: You have built every tool this unit uses. What is new here is doing it **without being told which tool** — the exam never labels a problem 'friction' or 'circular motion'. The recognition step is the skill: read the situation, decide what kind of problem it is, then execute the method you already know.

chunks.title: Recognise It: Four Problem Types
chunks.concept:
Almost every Unit 2 problem is one of four types. Learn to spot which from the **structure**, not from keywords.

| If the problem is about… | It is a… | Core move |
|---|---|---|
| one object speeding up / slowing down along a surface or a line (incline, rope pull, push at an angle) | **multi-force / Newton's second law** problem | FBD → axes along the acceleration → resolve off-axis forces → $\sum F = ma$ per axis |
| two or more objects pushing or pulling on **each other** | **interaction** problem | attribute each force to its source → third-law pairs (2 objects) vs balanced forces (1 object) → system then part |
| anything moving on a **curved path** at (roughly) constant speed | **circular-motion** problem | name the real inward force(s) → $\sum F_r = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ → limiting case |
| a **spring / stretch / force–extension** relationship or dataset | **Hooke's-law / graph** problem | $k$ = slope of the force–extension line → $F = kx$ → predict, stating the linear-range assumption |

==Two different problems can share numbers and still need different frameworks. The mass, the speed, and a coefficient could be a friction problem *or* a circular-motion problem — the giveaway is whether the path is straight or curved.==

After every solution, run the **reasonableness check**: units, a limiting case, the sign/direction, and whether the size is sensible.

workedExample.problem: Classify each, and name the first equation you would write. (a) 'A $3\text{ kg}$ block is pushed up a $20°$ ramp by a $25\text{ N}$ force parallel to the ramp; $\mu_k = 0.1$. Find its acceleration.' (b) 'A $0.5\text{ kg}$ ball on a $1.2\text{ m}$ string is swung in a horizontal circle at $4\text{ m/s}$. Find the tension.' (c) 'A $2\text{ kg}$ cart pushes a $3\text{ kg}$ cart across frictionless ice with a $10\text{ N}$ force on the pair. Find the force between the carts.' (d) 'Hanging $2\text{ N}$ stretches a spring $5\text{ cm}$. How far does $5\text{ N}$ stretch it?'

phases.label: (a)
steps: Structure: one object accelerating along an incline, with friction and an applied force. **Multi-force / Newton's second law** problem.
First equations: perpendicular axis $F_N = mg\cos\theta$ (to get friction), then along the ramp $\sum F_\parallel = F_{app} - mg\sin\theta - f_k = ma$.

phases.label: (b)
steps: Structure: motion on a curved (circular) path at constant speed. **Circular-motion** problem.
First equation: $F_T = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$ (the string tension is the whole centripetal force).

phases.label: (c)
steps: Structure: two objects pushing on each other. **Interaction** problem.
First equations: system $a = \dfrac{F_{ext}}{m_1 + m_2}$, then isolate the second cart: $F_{12} = m_2 a$.

phases.label: (d)
steps: Structure: a force–stretch proportionality with a dataset. **Hooke's-law / graph** problem.
First move: $k = \dfrac{F}{x} = \dfrac{2}{0.05} = 40\text{ N/m}$ (the slope), then $x = \dfrac{F}{k} = \dfrac{5}{40} = 0.125\text{ m}$, assuming the spring is still linear.

workedExample.keyMove: Reading the *structure* — one object on a line, objects on each other, a curved path, or a spring relationship — before touching the numbers.

formativeCheck.question: 'A $1000\text{ kg}$ car travels at $25\text{ m/s}$. The coefficient of friction with the road is $0.7$.' Which added sentence would make this a **circular-motion** problem rather than a straight-line friction problem?
choices: 'The driver brakes to a stop.'
'The road curves with a radius of $120\text{ m}$.'
'The car is on a $5°$ downhill slope.'
'The car tows a trailer.'

feedback.correct: Correct — a radius of curvature means the path is curved, so there is a centripetal acceleration $v^2/r$ and the question becomes whether friction can supply $mv^2/r$. The other additions keep the motion along a line (braking, a slope) or make it an interaction problem (the trailer).

incorrect.0: Braking is straight-line motion — a Newton's-second-law / friction problem along the direction of travel, no curvature.
incorrect.2: A downhill slope is an inclined-plane problem: still straight-line motion along the slope.
incorrect.3: Towing a trailer is a connected-objects (interaction) problem, still along a straight line.

hint: Circular motion needs a curved path. Which addition introduces a radius of curvature?
formativeCheck.solution: 'The road curves with a radius of $120\text{ m}$' — a curved path means a centripetal requirement $mv^2/r$.

chunks.title: Interaction Task: Attribute Every Force
chunks.concept:
When two or more objects act on each other, the recognition cue is **'on each other'** — a hand on a box, a box on a box, a rope between two carts, the ground on your feet.

The method:

1. **Attribute** every force to the object that exerts it ("the rope pulls the cart", "the Earth pulls the box"). If you cannot name the exerter, it is not a real force — drop it.
2. **Third-law pairs** act on **two different objects**, are the **same type** of interaction, and are always equal and opposite — even during a collision, even when the objects have very different masses. **Balanced forces** act on **one object** and happen to sum to zero.
3. Analyse the **system** first (external forces only → the common acceleration), then **isolate** one object to find an internal force.

==A force and 'the effect it causes' are not a third-law pair. Gravity on a book (down) and the table's normal force on the book (up) act on the *same* object — they are balanced forces, not partners. The partner of 'Earth pulls book down' is 'book pulls Earth up'.==

workedExample.problem: A $4.0\text{ kg}$ box (A) sits on top of a $6.0\text{ kg}$ box (B) on a frictionless floor. You push horizontally on B with $20\text{ N}$; the boxes move together (enough friction between A and B). Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$. (a) Find the acceleration. (b) Find the horizontal force B exerts on A, and name its third-law partner. (c) Is the normal force B exerts up on A a third-law pair with A's weight?

phases.label: (a) System
steps: External horizontal force on the A+B system: the $20\text{ N}$ push. Total mass $10\text{ kg}$.
$a = \dfrac{F_{ext}}{m_A + m_B} = \dfrac{20}{10} = 2.0\text{ m/s}^2$.

phases.label: (b) Isolate A
steps: The only horizontal force on A is friction from B. $\sum F_x = m_A a$: $f_{B\to A} = (4.0)(2.0) = 8.0\text{ N}$, forward.
Third-law partner: the friction force **A exerts backward on B**, also $8.0\text{ N}$ — same interaction, opposite object, opposite direction.

phases.label: (c) Normal force vs weight
steps: No. B's normal force up on A, and Earth's gravity down on A, both act **on A** — one object. They are (here) balanced forces, not a third-law pair.
The partner of 'B pushes A up' is 'A pushes B down' (same size). The partner of 'Earth pulls A down' is 'A pulls Earth up'.

phases.label: Check
steps: $f_{B\to A} = 8.0\text{ N} < 20\text{ N}$ push — the leftover $12\text{ N}$ accelerates B's own $6.0\text{ kg}$: $(6.0)(2.0) = 12\text{ N}$. ✓

workedExample.keyMove: Isolating the top box and realising the *only* horizontal force on it is friction from the box below — that friction is what accelerates it.

formativeCheck.question: A loaded truck and a small car collide head-on. During the collision, the force the truck exerts on the car compared with the force the car exerts on the truck is:
choices: much larger — the truck is more massive
exactly equal in magnitude and opposite in direction (Newton's third law), even though the car's acceleration is far greater
larger only if the truck was moving faster
zero on both, since they push equally and cancel

feedback.correct: Correct — the two forces are a third-law pair: equal magnitude, opposite direction, always, regardless of mass or speed. The car suffers a much bigger *acceleration* ($a = F/m$ with a small $m$), but the *forces* are identical in size.

incorrect.0: Mass changes the acceleration, not the interaction force. $F_{truck\to car} = F_{car\to truck}$ exactly.
incorrect.2: Speed does not break the third law either. The mutual forces are equal at every instant of contact.
incorrect.3: The forces act on *different objects*, so they do not cancel — each object feels its own force and accelerates.

hint: Third-law pairs act on two different objects and are always equal and opposite. Does mass or speed change that?
formativeCheck.solution: Equal and opposite (third law). The car's larger acceleration comes from its smaller mass, not a larger force.

chunks.title: Force Task: The Uncued Multi-Force Problem
chunks.concept:
The exam's hardest force problems combine an incline, friction, and an applied force at an angle — with no hint about method. The recognition cue: **one object, accelerating along a definite direction, several forces**.

The method never changes:

1. **Free-body diagram** — every real force, from its correct point of application.
2. **Axes along the acceleration.** On an incline, tilt them. On a banked curve, keep them horizontal/vertical. The rule: put one axis along the direction the object actually accelerates.
3. **Resolve** whatever forces are off-axis into components.
4. **$\sum F = ma$ on each axis** — the perpendicular axis (often $= 0$) usually gives the normal force; the motion axis gives the acceleration.
5. **Reasonableness check.**

==The single most common error: using $F_N = mg$ for the friction force on an incline or under an angled pull. Always get $F_N$ from the perpendicular-axis equation first.==

workedExample.problem: A $2.0\text{ kg}$ block is on a $30°$ incline. A rope pulls it **up the slope** with $18\text{ N}$, at $20°$ **above the incline surface**. $\mu_k = 0.15$ between block and incline; the block slides up. Take $g = 9.8\text{ m/s}^2$, $\sin 30° = 0.50$, $\cos 30° = 0.866$, $\sin 20° = 0.342$, $\cos 20° = 0.940$. Find the acceleration along the incline.

phases.label: Axes and components
steps: Axes: $x$ up the slope, $y$ perpendicular to the slope.
Rope: $T_x = 18\cos 20° = 16.9\text{ N}$ (up-slope), $T_y = 18\sin 20° = 6.16\text{ N}$ (away from surface).
Weight: $W_x = mg\sin 30° = (2.0)(9.8)(0.50) = 9.8\text{ N}$ (down-slope), $W_y = mg\cos 30° = (2.0)(9.8)(0.866) = 16.97\text{ N}$ (into surface).

phases.label: Perpendicular axis → normal force
steps: $\sum F_y = 0$: $F_N + T_y - W_y = 0 \Rightarrow F_N = W_y - T_y = 16.97 - 6.16 = 10.8\text{ N}$.
Note $F_N$ is well below $mg = 19.6\text{ N}$ — the incline *and* the rope's lift both reduce it.

phases.label: Friction and the motion axis
steps: Block slides up ⇒ kinetic friction acts down the slope: $f_k = \mu_k F_N = (0.15)(10.8) = 1.62\text{ N}$.
$\sum F_x = ma$: $T_x - W_x - f_k = ma \Rightarrow 16.9 - 9.8 - 1.62 = 5.48\text{ N}$.
$a = 5.48 / 2.0 = 2.7\text{ m/s}^2$ up the slope.

phases.label: Check
steps: Using $F_N = mg\cos\theta = 16.97\text{ N}$ (ignoring the rope's lift) would have given $f_k = 2.55\text{ N}$ and $a = 2.3\text{ m/s}^2$ — a real error. The perpendicular axis matters. ✓
Units and signs: net up-slope force positive, block accelerates up-slope. ✓

workedExample.keyMove: Doing the perpendicular axis first — with **both** the weight component and the rope's perpendicular component — to get the true $F_N$ before computing friction.

figure.caption: Free-body diagram for Step 1. Four forces: $mg$ from the centre, $F_N$ from the contact face (perpendicular), the rope tension $F_T$ from the block at $20^\circ$ above the surface, and kinetic friction $f_k$ from the contact face **down** the slope (the block slides up).

formativeCheck.question: A crate is dragged across level ground by a rope at $30°$ above horizontal. To find the friction force, you must first find the normal force, which is:
choices: $mg$ — the ground always supports the full weight
$mg - T\sin 30°$ — the rope's upward component carries part of the weight, so the ground supports less
$mg + T\sin 30°$ — the rope adds to the downward force
$T\cos 30°$ — the horizontal component of the tension

feedback.correct: Correct — vertical equilibrium: $F_N + T\sin 30° - mg = 0$, so $F_N = mg - T\sin 30°$. The rope lifts part of the weight, so the ground pushes up with less than $mg$, and the friction $\mu F_N$ is correspondingly smaller.

incorrect.0: Only true when all other forces are horizontal. Here the rope has an upward component that shares the load.
incorrect.2: The rope pulls *up* and forward, not down. Its vertical component subtracts from what the ground must supply.
incorrect.3: $T\cos 30°$ is horizontal — it has nothing to do with the vertical balance that sets $F_N$.

hint: Write $\sum F_y = 0$ with the normal force up, gravity down, and the rope's vertical component up. Solve for $F_N$.
formativeCheck.solution: $F_N = mg - T\sin 30°$ — the rope's upward pull reduces the normal force.

chunks.title: Graph Task: Read the Slope, Predict the Value
chunks.concept:
A force–extension (or force–deformation) dataset is a **graph problem**. Cue: a table or graph of force against stretch, or a spring described by how much it deforms under a load.

The method:

1. The relationship $F = kx$ is a **straight line through the origin**. Plot it (or picture it).
2. **$k$ is the slope** — rise over run, using any two points (or a best-fit line). Units N/m.
3. Once you have $k$, **predict**: $F = kx$ for a new stretch, or $x = F/k$ for a new force.
4. **State the assumption:** the prediction is valid only while the spring stays in its linear range (the data still fall on the straight line — it has not been over-stretched).

==$k$ is one fixed number for a given spring. A bigger force gives a proportionally bigger stretch, so the *ratio* $F/x$ — and the slope — does not change.==

This is the same graph-slope skill from Unit 1 kinematics ($a$ as the slope of $v$–$t$), reused.

workedExample.problem: A spring is loaded and its stretch recorded: $(2.0\text{ N}, 0.05\text{ m})$, $(4.0\text{ N}, 0.10\text{ m})$, $(6.0\text{ N}, 0.15\text{ m})$, $(8.0\text{ N}, 0.20\text{ m})$. (a) Find $k$. (b) Predict the stretch under $5.0\text{ N}$. (c) A student loads it with $50\text{ N}$ and predicts $x = 1.25\text{ m}$. Comment.

phases.label: (a) Slope
steps: The points are collinear through the origin. $k = \dfrac{\Delta F}{\Delta x} = \dfrac{8.0 - 2.0}{0.20 - 0.05} = \dfrac{6.0}{0.15} = 40\text{ N/m}$.
(Any single pair agrees: $2.0/0.05 = 40$.)

phases.label: (b) Predict
steps: $x = \dfrac{F}{k} = \dfrac{5.0}{40} = 0.125\text{ m}$, assuming the spring is still linear at $5.0\text{ N}$ (it is — that is within the tested range).

phases.label: (c) Comment
steps: The arithmetic ($50/40 = 1.25\text{ m}$) is fine, but $50\text{ N}$ is far outside the tested range ($\le 8.0\text{ N}$).
A real spring will exceed its elastic limit long before that — the line stops being straight, so $F = kx$ no longer applies and the prediction is unreliable.

phases.label: Check
steps: $k = 40\text{ N/m}$: the interactive's Spring Graph Explorer shows a line of exactly this slope. Predictions inside the data range are trustworthy; extrapolation far beyond it is not. ✓

workedExample.keyMove: Getting $k$ from the slope, then flagging that a prediction far outside the measured range assumes linearity that was never tested.

formativeCheck.question: A force–extension graph for a spring is a straight line from the origin through $(0.10\text{ m}, 3.0\text{ N})$, then it curves and flattens beyond $x = 0.10\text{ m}$. For a stretch of $0.06\text{ m}$, the force is:
choices: cannot be found

feedback.correct: Correct — $0.06\text{ m}$ is inside the straight-line (linear) region. There $k = 3.0/0.10 = 30\text{ N/m}$, so $F = kx = (30)(0.06) = 1.8\text{ N}$.

incorrect.1: $3.0\text{ N}$ is the force at $0.10\text{ m}$, not $0.06\text{ m}$. On the straight part, scale down: $0.06$ is $0.6 \times 0.10$, so $0.6 \times 3.0 = 1.8\text{ N}$.
incorrect.2: $5.0\text{ N}$ would require reading off the curved (non-linear) region, which is beyond $0.10\text{ m}$. At $0.06\text{ m}$ the spring is still linear.
incorrect.3: It can be found — $0.06\text{ m}$ is in the linear region, where $F = kx$ with $k$ from the slope.

hint: Is $0.06\text{ m}$ in the straight part of the graph or the curved part? On the straight part, $F = kx$ with $k$ = slope.
formativeCheck.solution: $k = 3.0/0.10 = 30\text{ N/m}$ in the linear region; $F = (30)(0.06) = 1.8\text{ N}$.

interactiveComponent.title: Free-Body Diagram Builder — All Scenarios
interactiveComponent.subtitle: Pick any scenario and build its diagram from scratch
interactiveComponent.description: The builder from Lessons 2, 3, 5, and 10, with every scenario available — level pushes, angled ropes, wall friction, spring forces, and the two $45°$ ramp cases. For each: decide which forces are present, set their directions, set their relative lengths, then **Check**. Use it to rehearse step 1 of every force problem — an FBD you can defend — before you write a single equation.

misconceptions.question: A student solves every Unit 2 problem by writing '$F = ma$' with $F$ equal to whichever force is named first in the problem. Why does this fail so often?
choices: It doesn't fail — the first-named force is always the net force.
$\vec{F}$ in $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$ is the **vector sum of all** forces on the object. You must draw the free-body diagram and combine every force (with direction) before applying the second law.
The problem should always use the last-named force instead.
$F = ma$ only works for objects at rest.

feedback.correct: Correct — the second law uses the *net* force: the vector sum of gravity, normal, friction, tension, applied pushes — everything acting on the chosen object. Skipping the FBD and grabbing one named force ignores the others and their directions.

incorrect.0: The first-named force is just one of several. On an incline with friction and a push, three forces act along the motion axis alone.
incorrect.2: There is no rule about naming order. Every real force on the object counts, whatever order the problem lists them.
incorrect.3: $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$ applies whether the object is at rest ($a = 0$) or accelerating. The point is that $\vec{F}$ is always the total.

hint: What does the $\vec{F}$ in $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$ actually stand for — one force, or all of them combined?
misconceptions.solution: $\vec{F}_{net}$ is the vector sum of every force on the object; you must build the FBD and combine them, not use a single named force.

misconceptions.question: On a synthesis FRQ, which of these is a sign that a student has picked the **wrong framework** for a problem about a car on a curved, flat road?
choices: They write $\sum F_r = mv^2/r$ with friction as the inward force.
They set the net force to zero 'because the speed is constant', concluding the car is in equilibrium.
They note that the normal force equals $mg$ because the road is flat.
They check the limiting case $v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g r}$.

feedback.correct: Correct — constant *speed* on a curve is **not** equilibrium: the velocity direction changes, so there is a centripetal acceleration and a non-zero net force pointing inward. Treating it as equilibrium is the wrong framework and gives the wrong answer.

incorrect.0: That is exactly right for this problem — the correct framework.
incorrect.2: On a flat road with only vertical forces besides friction, $F_N = mg$ is correct.
incorrect.3: Checking $v_{\max} = \sqrt{\mu_s g r}$ is a good limiting-case check for this framework.

hint: Is an object moving at constant speed around a curve in equilibrium? What is happening to its velocity vector?
misconceptions.solution: Setting $\sum F = 0$ 'because speed is constant' — a curved path has a centripetal acceleration, so the net force is non-zero and inward.

errorAnalysis.studentWork:
**Problem:** a $0.40\text{ kg}$ ball on a $0.80\text{ m}$ string is swung in a **vertical** circle. At the **top** of the circle its speed is $4.0\text{ m/s}$. Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$. Find the string tension at the top.

**Student's work:** 'At the top, tension is up and gravity is down. The ball moves in a circle at constant speed, so it's in equilibrium: $F_T = mg = (0.40)(10) = 4.0\text{ N}$.'
prompts: Identify the two errors (one about the framework, one about a direction).
State the correct principle and the direction of 'toward the centre' at the top.
errorAnalysis.modelResponse:
1. Framework error: the ball is **not in equilibrium** — it is in circular motion, accelerating toward the centre at $v^2/r$. Direction error: at the top of a vertical circle, 'toward the centre' points **downward**, and the string (running from the ball up to the centre... no — the ball is at the top, the centre is below it, so the string pulls the ball **down**, toward the centre). Both the tension and gravity point down at the top.
2. Correct principle: $\sum F_r = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$, with the positive direction toward the centre (downward at the top). Both $F_T$ and $mg$ are in that direction: $F_T + mg = \dfrac{mv^2}{r}$.
3. $F_T = \dfrac{mv^2}{r} - mg = \dfrac{(0.40)(4.0)^2}{0.80} - (0.40)(10) = \dfrac{6.4}{0.80} - 4.0 = 8.0 - 4.0 = 4.0\text{ N}$.
4. The number happens to match the student's, but the reasoning was wrong: had the speed been $3.0\text{ m/s}$, the correct tension would be $\dfrac{(0.40)(9)}{0.80} - 4.0 = 4.5 - 4.0 = 0.5\text{ N}$, while the fake-equilibrium method would still say $4.0\text{ N}$. Reasonableness: at the minimum top speed $v = \sqrt{gr} = \sqrt{8} = 2.83\text{ m/s}$, tension would be zero — gravity alone provides $mv^2/r$. At $4.0\text{ m/s}$ we are above that, so a small positive tension ($4.0\text{ N}$) is sensible. ✓

representationConnections: This lesson is entirely about moving between representations under time pressure: reading a **verbal** scenario and classifying it; translating to a **free-body diagram**; choosing **axes** and resolving into components; writing the **equations** ($\sum F = ma$, $\sum F_r = mv^2/r$, $F = kx$); reading a **graph** slope; and running back to a **limiting case** or a **motion diagram** to check. The unifying principle across all four problem types is the same one the unit opened with: define the object, find the net force, and $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$.

lessonAssessment.question: Two planets have the same radius, but planet Y has four times the mass of planet X. An object's weight on Y compared with its weight on X is:
choices: the same
twice as much
four times as much
sixteen times as much

feedback.correct: Correct — surface gravity $g = GM/R^2$. Same $R$, four times $M$ ⇒ four times $g$ ⇒ four times the weight $mg$ for the same object.

incorrect.0: Weight depends on the local $g$, which depends on the planet's mass. More mass, more weight.
incorrect.1: $g \propto M$ at fixed radius, so four times the mass gives four times $g$, not two.
incorrect.3: That would be $M^2$ or a radius effect. Here only $M$ changes, linearly: $\times 4$.

hint: Surface gravity $g = GM/R^2$. If $R$ is unchanged and $M \to 4M$, what happens to $g$ (and hence to $mg$)?
lessonAssessment.solution: $g \propto M/R^2$; same $R$, $4\times M$ ⇒ $4\times g$ ⇒ four times the weight.

lessonAssessment.question: On a frictionless table, a $3.0\text{ kg}$ block is connected over a pulley to a $2.0\text{ kg}$ block that hangs. Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$. The acceleration of the system is:

feedback.correct: Correct — the only external force driving the system is the weight of the hanging block, $m_2 g = 20\text{ N}$; the total mass being accelerated is $m_1 + m_2 = 5.0\text{ kg}$. $a = \dfrac{m_2 g}{m_1 + m_2} = \dfrac{20}{5.0} = 4.0\text{ m/s}^2$.

incorrect.0: The hanging block is not in free fall — the rope tension holds it back. Only if the table block had zero mass would $a = g$.
incorrect.2: $6.7\text{ m/s}^2$ is $m_2 g / m_1 = 20/3$ — dividing by the wrong mass. The whole system (both blocks) is accelerating.
incorrect.3: $2.0\text{ m/s}^2$ divides by the wrong thing. $a = m_2 g/(m_1+m_2) = 20/5 = 4.0\text{ m/s}^2$.

hint: Treat both blocks as one system. External driving force = weight of the hanging block. Total mass = both blocks.

lessonAssessment.question: A ball on a string hangs from the ceiling of a car. When the car turns a corner at steady speed, the string hangs at an angle, tilted toward the **outside** of the turn. The horizontal component of the string tension:
choices: points outward, balancing a centrifugal force
points toward the centre of the turn, and provides the ball's centripetal force $mv^2/r$
is zero — the ball is in equilibrium
points backward, opposing the car's motion

feedback.correct: Correct — the string tilts so that its horizontal component points **toward the centre** of the turn (even though the ball itself is displaced toward the outside). That inward component is the net horizontal force and equals $mv^2/r$; the vertical component balances gravity. $\tan\theta = v^2/(rg)$ — the same relation as a banked curve or a conical pendulum.

incorrect.0: The ball is displaced outward, but the *force* on it from the string points inward. There is no centrifugal force in the ground frame.
incorrect.2: The ball accelerates toward the centre of the turn, so it is not in equilibrium — there is a net inward horizontal force.
incorrect.3: At steady speed there is no forward or backward acceleration, so no horizontal force along the direction of motion. The net horizontal force is perpendicular to the motion, toward the centre.

hint: The ball moves in a circle (the car's turn), so it needs a net force toward the centre. Which component of the tension can supply that?
lessonAssessment.solution: The horizontal component of the tension points toward the centre of the turn and equals $mv^2/r$; $\tan\theta = v^2/(rg)$.

lessonAssessment.scenario: A $2.0\text{ kg}$ box is on a $37°$ incline. A light rope, parallel to the incline surface, runs up the slope, over a frictionless pulley at the top, and down to a hanging $1.5\text{ kg}$ mass. The coefficient of kinetic friction between box and incline is $\mu_k = 0.20$. The system is released and the hanging mass descends, dragging the box up the incline. Take $g = 10\text{ m/s}^2$, $\sin 37° = 0.60$, $\cos 37° = 0.80$.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Draw a free-body diagram for the box and a separate one for the hanging mass. On the box diagram, mark which axis you will use for Newton's second law and why.
parts.modelResponse: Box: weight $mg$ down, normal force $F_N$ perpendicular to the incline, tension $F_T$ up the slope, kinetic friction $f_k$ **down** the slope (the box moves up, so friction opposes that). Axes tilted to the incline; the box accelerates along the slope, so the motion axis is along the incline (up-slope positive). Hanging mass: tension $F_T$ up, weight $m_2 g$ down; it accelerates downward.

figures.caption: The box (four forces; $f_k$ points **down** the slope because the box is dragged **up**) and the hanging mass (tension up, weight down — weight wins, so it descends).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the normal force on the box and the kinetic friction force.
parts.modelResponse: Perpendicular axis for the box: $F_N = mg\cos 37° = (2.0)(10)(0.80) = 16\text{ N}$. Friction: $f_k = \mu_k F_N = (0.20)(16) = 3.2\text{ N}$, directed down the slope.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Write Newton's second law for each object (taking the direction of motion as positive) and solve for the acceleration.
parts.modelResponse: Box (up-slope positive): $F_T - mg\sin 37° - f_k = m_1 a \Rightarrow F_T - (2.0)(10)(0.60) - 3.2 = 2.0a \Rightarrow F_T - 15.2 = 2.0a$. Hanging mass (downward positive): $m_2 g - F_T = m_2 a \Rightarrow 15 - F_T = 1.5a$. Add: $15 - 15.2 = 3.5a \Rightarrow a = -0.057\text{ m/s}^2$.

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Interpret the sign of your acceleration. Does the system actually move as described? Justify.
parts.modelResponse: The acceleration comes out slightly negative ($\approx -0.06\text{ m/s}^2$), meaning the assumed motion (hanging mass down, box up) cannot be sustained — the driving weight $m_2 g = 15\text{ N}$ is essentially balanced by $mg\sin\theta + f_k = 15.2\text{ N}$. Released from rest, the system stays at rest (static friction, which can be at least as large as $f_k$, holds it): $15\text{ N}$ is not enough to overcome $mg\sin\theta + f_{s} $. The scenario's 'the hanging mass descends' does not occur.

lessonAssessment.scoringNotes: (a) 1 pt box forces all present and correctly directed (friction down-slope, justified by up-slope motion), 1 pt hanging-mass diagram, 1 pt names the incline-aligned motion axis. (b) 1 pt $F_N = mg\cos\theta = 16\text{ N}$ (not $mg$), 1 pt $f_k = 3.2\text{ N}$. (c) 1 pt each correct N2L equation, 1 pt combine and solve $a \approx -0.06\text{ m/s}^2$ (accept $-0.05$ to $-0.06$). (d) 1 pt recognises the negative result means the assumed motion fails, 1 pt concludes the system stays at rest with a supporting argument. Full credit for a student who instead argues at part (c) that the system won't move and computes the static check.

figures.caption: Set-up. Box: gravity down, $F_N$ perpendicular to the surface, rope tension $F_T$ up the slope, kinetic friction $f_k$ **down** the slope (the box is dragged **up**). Hanging mass: tension up, weight down.

examConnection: The unit test bank and the exam interleave these four problem types with no labels. Practice the **recognition** step explicitly: for each problem, name the type ('multi-force', 'interaction', 'circular', 'graph') and the first equation before computing anything. The highest-value habits from the whole unit: define the object and draw its FBD before writing $\vec{F}_{net} = m\vec{a}$; get $F_N$ from the perpendicular axis, never assume $F_N = mg$; keep third-law pairs (two objects) distinct from balanced forces (one object); treat 'centripetal' as a direction, not a force; and read $k$ as a slope.
summary:
- **Four problem types**, recognised by structure: multi-force (one object, a line or incline), interaction (objects on each other), circular (curved path), graph (force–extension).
- **Multi-force:** FBD → axes along the acceleration → resolve → $\sum F = ma$ per axis. Get $F_N$ from the perpendicular axis first.
- **Interaction:** attribute every force to its source; third-law pairs act on two objects, balanced forces on one; system then part.
- **Circular:** name the real inward force(s); $\sum F_r = mv^2/r$; check a limiting case. Constant speed on a curve is *not* equilibrium.
- **Graph:** $k$ = slope of the force–extension line; $F = kx$; state the linear-range assumption.
- **Always** finish with a reasonableness check: units, limiting case, sign, size.

exitQuestion.question: A student solves four Unit 2 problems and gets: (i) a block on a frictionless $30°$ incline accelerating at $9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ down the slope; (ii) a normal force on an incline larger than $mg$; (iii) a car rounding a curve with the friction pointing away from the centre; (iv) a spring constant that comes out negative. How many of these results are physically impossible or clearly wrong?
choices: one
two
three
all four

feedback.correct: Correct — all four fail a reasonableness check. (i) On a frictionless $30°$ incline $a = g\sin 30° = 4.9\text{ m/s}^2$, not $9.8$ (that would be free fall). (ii) $F_N = mg\cos\theta < mg$ on an incline — it cannot exceed $mg$ without an extra downward push. (iii) Friction on a car rounding a curve points *toward* the centre — it is the centripetal force. (iv) A spring constant is always positive; a negative $k$ would mean a spring that pushes away from its natural length.

incorrect.0: More than one is wrong. Check each against a limiting case or a known sign.
incorrect.1: Still more are wrong — check the incline acceleration against $g\sin\theta$ and the friction direction on a curve.
incorrect.2: One more is also wrong: a normal force on a plain incline cannot exceed $mg$.

hint: Take each result to a limiting case or a known bound: what is $a$ on a frictionless incline? Can $F_N$ exceed $mg$ with no extra downward force? Which way does friction point on a curve? Can $k$ be negative?
exitQuestion.solution: All four are wrong: (i) $a = g\sin\theta = 4.9\text{ m/s}^2$; (ii) $F_N = mg\cos\theta < mg$; (iii) friction points toward the centre; (iv) $k > 0$ always.
